{{Short description|Number theory related to prime numbers}}
[[File:Chebyshev bias.svg|thumb|Plot of the function <math>\pi(x;4,3)-\pi(x;4,1)</math> for ''n''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;30000]]
In [[number theory]], '''Chebyshev's bias''' is the phenomenon that most of the time, there are more [[prime number|prime]]s of the form 4''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;3 than of the form 4''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, up to the same limit. This phenomenon was first observed by Russian mathematician [[Pafnuty Chebyshev]] in 1853.

==Description==
Let {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;''n'',&nbsp;''m'') denote the number of primes of the form ''nk''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''m'' up to&nbsp;''x''. By the [[prime number theorem]] (extended to [[Prime number theorem#Prime_number_theorem_for_arithmetic_progressions|arithmetic progressions]]),

:<math>\pi(x;4,1)\sim\pi(x;4,3)\sim \frac{1}{2}\frac{x}{\ln x}.</math>

That is, half of the primes are of the form 4''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, and half of the form 4''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;3. A reasonable guess would be that {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;1)&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;3) and {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;1)&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;3) each also occur 50% of the time. This, however, is not supported by numerical evidence — in fact, {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;3)&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;1) occurs much more frequently. For example, this inequality holds for all primes ''x''&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;26833 except 5, 17, 41 and 461, for which {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;1)&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;3). The first ''x'' such that {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;1)&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;3) is 26861, that is, {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;3)&nbsp;&ge;&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;1) for all ''x''&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;26861.

In general, if 0&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;''a'', ''b''&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;''n'' are integers, [[greatest common divisor|gcd]](''a'',&nbsp;''n'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;gcd(''b'',&nbsp;''n'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, ''a'' is a [[quadratic residue]] [[Modular arithmetic|mod]] ''n'', ''b'' is a quadratic nonresidue mod ''n'', then {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;''n'',&nbsp;''b'')&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;''n'',&nbsp;''a'') occurs more often than not. This has been proved only by assuming strong forms of the [[Riemann hypothesis]]. The stronger conjecture of [[Stanisław Knapowski|Knapowski]] and [[Pál Turán|Turán]], that the [[natural density|density]] of the numbers&nbsp;''x'' for which {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;3)&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;4,&nbsp;1) holds is&nbsp;1 (that is, it holds for [[almost all]] ''x''), turned out to be false. They, however, do have a [[logarithmic density]], which is approximately 0.9959....<ref>(Rubinstein—Sarnak, 1994)</ref>

==Generalizations==

This is for ''k'' = −4 to find the smallest prime ''p'' such that <math>\sum_{q \le p,\ q\ \text{is prime}}\left(\frac{k}{q}\right)>0</math> (where <math>\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)</math> is the [[Kronecker symbol]]), however, for a given nonzero integer ''k'' (not only ''k'' = −4), we can also find the smallest prime ''p'' satisfying this condition. By the prime number theorem, for every nonzero integer ''k'', there are infinitely many primes ''p'' satisfying this condition.

For positive integers ''k'' = 1, 2, 3, ..., the smallest primes ''p'' are

:2, 11100143, 61981, 3, 2082927221, 5, 2, 11100143, 2, 3, 577, 61463, 2083, 11, 2, 3, 2, 11100121, 5, 2082927199, 1217, 3, 2, 5, 2, 17, 61981, 3, 719, 7, 2, 11100143, 2, 3, 23, 5, 11, 31, 2, 3, 2, 13, 17, 7, 2082927199, 3, 2, 61463, 2, 11100121, 7, 3, 17, 5, 2, 11, 2, 3, 31, 7, 5, 41, 2, 3, ... {{oeis|A326615}}

For negative integers ''k'' = −1, −2, −3, ..., the smallest primes ''p'' are

:2, 3, 608981813029, 26861, 7, 5, 2, 3, 2, 11, 5, 608981813017, 19, 3, 2, 26861, 2, 643, 11, 3, 11, 31, 2, 5, 2, 3, 608981813029, 48731, 5, 13, 2, 3, 2, 7, 11, 5, 199, 3, 2, 11, 2, 29, 53, 3, 109, 41, 2, 608981813017, 2, 3, 13, 17, 23, 5, 2, 3, 2, 1019, 5, 263, 11, 3, 2, 26861, ... {{oeis|A392284}}

For fundamental [[Discriminant of an algebraic number field|discriminants]] of real [[Quadratic field|quadratic fields]] (''k'' = 1, 5, 8, 12, 13, 17, 21, 24, 28, 29, 33, 37, 40, 41, 44, 53, 56, 57, 60, 61, ... {{oeis|A003658}}), the smallest primes ''p'' are

:2, 2082927221, 11100143, 61463, 2083, 2, 1217, 5, 3, 719, 2, 11, 3, 2, 7, 17, 11, 2, 7, 5, 2, 13, 2, 3, 23, 7, 3, 2, 13, 19, 2, 23, 17, 2, 5, 2, 7, 3, 2, 13, 3, 2, 19, 7, 2, 31, 31, 5, 17, 2, 13, 13, 3, 47, 2, 5, 3, 2, 37, 2, 47, 2, 5, 7, 2, 43, 2, 3, 11, 5, 3, 2, 29, ... {{oeis|A306499}}

For fundamental discriminants of imaginary quadratic fields (''k'' = −3, −4, −7, −8, −11, −15, −19, −20, −23, −24, −31, −35, −39, −40, −43, −47, −51, −52, −55, −56, −59, ... {{oeis|A003657}}), the smallest primes ''p'' are

:608981813029, 26861, 2, 3, 5, 2, 11, 3, 2, 5, 2, 11, 2, 11, 53, 2, 13, 17, 2, 3, 5, 163, 3, 2, 2, 11, 5, 2, 31, 31, 2, 2, 3, 23, 2, 41, 3, 2, 13, 47, 2, 5, 19, 7, 11, 2, 191, 2, 3, 19, 2, 15073, 3, 2, 29, 5, 2, 41, 109, 2, 11, 2, 31, 59, 3, 2, 19, 2, 11, 53, 2, 1019, 137, ... {{oeis|A306500}}

For every (positive or negative) [[square number|nonsquare]] integer ''k'', there are more primes ''p'' with <math>\left(\frac{k}{p}\right)=-1</math> than with <math>\left(\frac{k}{p}\right)=1</math> (up to the same limit) more often than not.

==Extension to higher power residue==

Let ''m'' and ''n'' be integers such that ''m''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0, ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, gcd(''m'',&nbsp;''n'') =&nbsp;1, define a [[function (mathematics)|function]] <math display=block>f(m,n)=\sum_{p \text{ is prime, } p\,\mid\,\varphi(n),\ x^p \,\equiv\, m \pmod n \text{ has a solution }} \left(\frac{1}{p}\right), </math> where <math>\varphi</math> is the [[Euler's totient function]].

For example, ''f''(1, 5) = ''f''(4, 5) = 1/2, ''f''(2, 5) = ''f''(3, 5) = 0, ''f''(1, 6) = 1/2, ''f''(5, 6) = 0, ''f''(1, 7) = 5/6, ''f''(2, 7) = ''f''(4, 7) = 1/2, ''f''(3, 7) = ''f''(5, 7) = 0, ''f''(6, 7) = 1/3, ''f''(1, 8) = 1/2, ''f''(3, 8) = ''f''(5, 8) = ''f''(7, 8) = 0, ''f''(1, 9) = 5/6, ''f''(2, 9) = ''f''(5, 9) = 0, ''f''(4, 9) = ''f''(7, 9) = 1/2, ''f''(8, 9) = 1/3.

It is conjectured that if 0&nbsp;<&nbsp;''a'', ''b''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''n'' are integers, gcd(''a'',&nbsp;''n'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;gcd(''b'',&nbsp;''n'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, ''f''(''a'', ''n'') > ''f''(''b'', ''n''), then {{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;''n'',&nbsp;''b'')&nbsp;>&nbsp;{{pi}}(''x'';&nbsp;''n'',&nbsp;''a'') occurs more often than not.
